articles.headline: Epic Games’ ‘Unreal Engine AI MegaJam’ contest will reward cash for AI vibe-coded slop games that no one asked for
keyFacts: Epic Games announced the Unreal Engine AI MegaJam contest, inviting teams to use AI tools and coding agents to build playable games for cash prizes.
Epic Games stated that top category winners will receive $7,500, and standout entries can earn development continuation grants of up to $50,000.
The game jam event is scheduled to commence early next month.
body: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney’s all-in on shoveling AI “vibe coding” into game dev has reached a new embarrassing low today, somehow.

Following up on last week’s Epic Games Store redesign that was “vibe-coded” and slopped together , the Fortnite publisher is now asking people to “team with up to four other humans and unlimited agents to build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN), and compete for cash prizes.”
Image via Epic Games This is not a joke post. It feels like ragebait, but it appears to be genuine.

So, basically, not only is Epic all-in on using AI to make games for them, they are now hoping that other people will do it in their stead for some comparatively measly prizes ($7,500 each for top placement in three different categories).

“Jam online from anywhere, with your local game dev community, or in person in San Francisco at Digital Jungle, where you’ll build alongside teams from Anthropic, Google, Meshy, OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and more,” Epic said. “Bring any AI tools into your workflow, from asset generation to coding agents. Get creative! Prototype the mechanic you never had time for, or try the art style you weren’t sure you could pull off.”

Epic said that “standout Unreal Engine and UEFN entries can earn development continuation grants of up to $50,000 to keep building after the jam, so the momentum doesn’t stop when the jam ends,” but the jam commences early next month.

Honestly? I don’t really have anything nice to say about this. So I’ll leave it to one of the top replies on the Unreal Engine account’s announcement today, which fittingly includes an AI-generated image of a hand that has six fingers:
Like do you guys have a humiliation kink or something
— Lexi (@LexisSketchbook) October 22, 2026
The rest of the replies are filled to the brim with the same sentiment, so I hope gamers are ready to stand up for what they believe in when it comes to Epic, Unreal, and UEFN.

articles.headline: Everything We Know About the PS6, Sony’s Next-Gen Console
keyFacts: Reports indicate that the PlayStation 6 will likely cost at least $1,000 due to high memory costs driven by the AI data center boom.
Sony announced it will end production of physical PlayStation game discs in January 2028, making PS6 games digital only.
Sony has not set a release date for the PS6, but memory shortages have led reports to suggest a possible release in 2028 or 2029.
body: What is time? It feels like PlayStation 5 was released yesterday, but it’s actually almost six years old. This is usually when we can expect to start hearing more about a console’s successor. Seven years is a typical console generation lifespan; no PlayStation has ever been released more than seven years after its predecessor, and the eight-year gaps between Switch and Switch 2, or Xbox 360 and Xbox One, are the longest ever for a home console. (Both pale next to the Game Boy’s incredible 12-year run, though.)

If it doesn’t feel like it’s time to start thinking about the PlayStation 6 yet, it’s because lengthening game development times have slowed the pace of new releases for PS5, because initial take-up of the console was slowed by supply issues, and because the COVID-19 pandemic distorted everyone’s sense of time. But the time is upon us all the same.

As it happens, there are reasons why the PS5 could keep going for a few years yet. But regardless, Sony is surely already planning for the next PlayStation, and considering how it’s going to extend PS5’s dominance of the dedicated home console market and crushing defeat of Xbox into the next generation. Here’s what we know so far.
What is the latest PS6 news?

Reports suggest that the PS6 is headed for a very high price point, albeit not quite as high as the next Xbox. Trusted tech leaker Kepler_L2 says that the RAM and NAND memory alone for the PS6 currently costs over $680, a result of the mass shortage in computer memory during the current AI data center boom. That would likely put the price of the PS6 at around $1,000. Read our full report.

PS6 won't, however, cost quite as much as the next Xbox. Kepler_L2 says that the cost of all the components for the PS6 (known as the bill of materials, or "BOM") is "approximately $200 lower" than for the next Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix. Reports say that Microsoft projects Helix's price will land between $1,200 and $1,800. Again, this supports a $1,000-plus price tag for Sony's next console, perhaps at the lower end of that range.
What is PS6’s release date? When is it coming out?

We don’t know, and we’re probably a long way from knowing. Until recently, it seemed that a November 2027 release for the PlayStation 6 was on the cards, if not actually the plan, following the pattern established by the PS3, PS4, and PS5.

But the RAM crisis has changed that. Sony has been open that it has not set a release date for PS6, and that memory shortages are the reason. Reportedly, Sony is now looking at 2028 or even 2029 as a possible release date for the new console.
Why might PS6 be delayed?
As well as the current difficulty of securing enough chips and setting a reasonable price point, there are other reasons Sony might choose to wait before releasing the PS6.

The PS5 has sold well, on par with the PS4, but it has done so in what appears to be a shrinking overall market for dedicated home consoles. The adoption rate for the current generation has been slow, with the biggest games like Fortnite, Roblox, and Minecraft still very playable on older hardware. Lengthening game development cycles (also impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic) mean that current hardware feels underexploited; GTA 6, bound to be the PS5’s defining game, hasn’t been released yet. Meanwhile, diminishing returns from technological advances are clashing with the ballooning cost of developing games for current specs.

All of these are reasons why consumer demand for another generation of PlayStation is probably on the low side — and why, as Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier put it, a 2027 release for PS6 would be “a disaster for everyone involved.”
What will PS6’s price be?

At the moment, it's looking as though PlayStation 6 will cost at least $1,000. Reports have put the cost of the new console's memory alone at more than $680. It is estimated to be cheaper to make than the next Xbox by around $200 — but the next Xbox will reportedly cost between $1,200 and $1,800, according to Microsoft's own projections.

Demand for microchips amid the AI data center boom, as well as inflation and general economic factors, are driving the price of electronics up sharply. Earlier generations of PlayStation saw their prices reduced over their lifespans, but the PS5 costs more now than it did at launch, and the PS5 Pro has hit $900.
Sony is evidently concerned about pricing for PS6; in May 2026, it told investors that it was even considering "changing business models" for its next console.
Will PS6 have a disc drive?

It seems not — or not out of the box, at any rate. Sony has announced that it will end production of physical PlayStation game discs in January 2028. With the PS6 not expected to arrive until 2028 at the earliest, it's a given that PS6 games will be digital only, and highly probable that the console won't include a disc drive.

However, it's still possible that Sony will sell an external disc drive module for the PS6, as it does for PS5. This would ensure backward-compatibility with players' libraries of physical PS4 and PS5 games, as well as allowing Blu-ray playback.
What games will PS6 have?

It’s very hard to say what games PS6 will have at this point, not least because of the potential delay to its launch. Although games planned for PS6 are almost certainly already in development, most developers — Sony itself included — will be keeping their options open in terms of platform while they wait to see when the new console will arrive.

Here’s an example: When Sony-owned developer Insomniac was hacked in 2023, its future development roadmap leaked, including proposed dates for Marvel’s Spider-Man 3 in 2028 and Marvel’s X-Men in 2030. Who knows if these dates remain accurate — a 2025 Venom game didn’t materialize, but Marvel’s Wolverine hit its planned 2026 launch.

Assuming they are, Spider-Man 3 was probably planned as a PS6 game. If PS6 doesn’t launch until 2028 or 2029, will Insomniac delay Spider-Man 3, shift it to PS5, or go for a cross-gen launch? All seem plausible.
We can safely assume Marvel’s X-Men will be a PS6 game, though. So that’s one!

There are a bunch of other contenders, all unconfirmed, including Gran Turismo 8, a new Astro Bot game, an unannounced title in development at Naughty Dog (not thought to be The Last of Us Part 3), and whatever Santa Monica Studio is currently making. All of these could go to PS5, PS6, or both.
And what about Grand Theft Auto 7? Well, given how long it is taking Rockstar Games to make GTA 6, it might be safer to earmark GTA 7 for PS7. Or maybe PS8.
What will the PS6 controller be like?

There's no firm information on the PS6's gamepad, although Sony has filed a number of game-controller patents recently. These suggest Sony is experimenting with some kind of modular, customizable layout, including a touchscreen interface, or perhaps a controller that will eschew buttons completely, in favor of a haptic touch interface. Another patent explores the idea of using NFC communication in the controller to simplify payments.

Companies often use patents to legally lock down ideas they are just exploring, so it shouldn't be assumed that any of this technology will be in the final PS6 controller. A controller without physical buttons is particularly unlikely. But the patents give some idea of the concepts Sony is exploring for its next gamepad.
Will PS6 be backward-compatible?
At last, here’s a question we can answer with a degree of certainty. It’s highly likely that the PS6 will be backward-compatible with PS5 games, and probably PS4 games, too.

Like Microsoft, Sony has announced that it’s going to continue to work with chip supplier AMD on the processors for its future hardware. Reports suggest that the PS6 will use a next-gen Zen processor that’s compatible with the x86 architecture used in PS4 and PS5, making backward compatibility easy to implement.

Backward compatibility has also become an expectation among players, who have become used to bringing their game libraries forward onto new hardware. It’s arguably a necessity for Sony and its partners, too. The pace of game development has slowed enough that the PS5 would have really struggled for software in its first few years if it hadn’t also been able to play PS4 games.
What are PS6’s tech specs? How powerful will it be?

There have been a few unconfirmed leaks about the PS6’s specs, although as yet there’s nothing quite substantial enough to treat as gospel. All we know for sure is that AMD will once again supply the silicon.
That being said, we can expect the processor will be a custom iteration of AMD’s next-gen Zen 6 chip. Similarly, the new RDNA 5 graphics unit from AMD will likely form the basis of the PS6’s GPU.
Some have suggested that the console will have as much as 30 GB of GDDR7 RAM, but there doesn’t seem to be enough evidence to support this yet.

Most agree on the target performance of the spec, though: the PS6 should be capable of 4K gaming at 120 frames per second with advanced ray tracing. (This doesn’t mean that all games will run at this level, though — far from it!)
What about the next-gen PlayStation handheld?

This is a whole separate topic, really, but it’s worth mentioning here. Sony is widely reported to be working on a handheld PlayStation to compete with Nintendo’s Switch 2 as well as the Steam Deck, Xbox Ally, and other PC handhelds.

The key question about this device is its level of compatibility with the PlayStation catalog. Full PS4 compatibility would seem to be a given, and most reports suggest the handheld will be able to run PS5 games too — if not necessarily all of them, or at the same quality as PS5.

In fact, some level of PS6 compatibility is even possible, because the handheld is rumored to use a cut-down version of the same Zen 6 and RDNA 5 architecture employed in PS6. With increasing overlap between hardware generations being a trend, and with third-party games needing to run on a very wide range of hardware (factoring in PC and, sometimes, Switch and Switch 2), there’s a chance that the handheld PlayStation will be able to keep pace with its biggest brother for some time.
Check out this Digital Foundry report for lots more detail on the topic of the PlayStation handheld.

articles.headline: Simone Biles gets emotional about selling Houston-area home with Jonathan Owens
keyFacts: Gymnast Simone Biles and NFL player Jonathan Owens sold their Spring, Texas home after owning it for over six years.
Biles stated in a TikTok video that she became emotional and cried while preparing the property to go on the market.
The property sold in four days for a price between $1.08 million and $1.24 million according to real estate records.
body: Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens are saying goodbye to their Spring, Texas home.

The Olympian shared that she and Owens have sold the home that she and the NFL star had for over six years and reminisced about all the memories they had there. Biles shared in a TikTok video on Tuesday, Oct. 22, as she got emotional about the process.

“Today is the first day the house is going to be on the market,” Biles said. “Why the f--- am I boohoo crying? F---. This house will be on the market for the first time, and I don’t know why I’m boohoo crying.”

@simonebilesowens the house sold in 4 days 😭 I was so excited to put in air freshners for the potential buyers & showing Jonathan the last look. I just cried instead… anyone else? #emotionallyattached ♬ original sound - Simone Biles

“I was here for six years, and I feel like there were just so many good memories, so many bad memories,” she continued. “But I feel like I grew up in this house. It’s made me a real adult, so I’m gonna miss it. Ugh, I didn’t think I’d be emotional about a house.”

In the video, Biles took fans on a tour of the house where the rooms were bare with no furniture, as well as the backyard, which included a swimming pool. Towards the end of the video, the Olympian got teary-eyed again, sharing how much she wants the house to be as special to them as it was to her.
“Whoever buys this house, I hope it brings you as much joy as it did for me,” she concluded.

The home sold between $1.08 million and $1.24 million, according to the Houston Association of Realtors, per KHOU. She bought the home in 2020, and according to her caption, it sold in four days. The home was listed on Sept. 26 and closed on Oct. 15. It has four bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, and sits on over 1 acre of land.

Prior to this home update, Owens and Biles -- who got married in 2023 -- shared last year that they finished building their waterfront mansion in November 2025. The home is located in the Spring/Greater Houston area and is complete with a laundry room with four machines, a dog room, a primary bedroom with a cozy fireplace, and an in-ground trampoline for the Olympian to jump in the comfort of her own home.

articles.headline: Bournemouth v Milan, Celtic v Celta Vigo, and more: Europa League – live
keyFacts: Bournemouth led Milan during the match, with Marcus Tavernier scoring a penalty to make it 2-0.
Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan received a red card for pushing Tyler Adams following a corner kick.
Substitute goalkeeper Lorenzo Torriani entered the game for Milan after the red card incident.
body: Bournemouth are enjoying themselves, I think, knocking the ball about in midfield and making Milan run. Which I expect they can do as, dreadful though his time at Man United was, Ruben Amorim had the players fit and one of the various reasons they’re so dreadful now is they’re no longer at the same physical level.

Pino has the ball in the net for Palace, turning home adroitly after a ball inside the full-back releases Khalili, who picks him out with a cut-back. The ref immediately disallows it for an offside against Khalaili, but I think this’ll be overturned by VAR – he was on.
Hassan nashes down the left, cuts back, and Baur meets it on the burst, cracking low and too hard for Radu, who gets a hand to it but can’t keep it out.
45 min: “Given that his pops Patrick once played for Milan,” writes Peter Oh, “couldn’t Justin Kluivert have toned down his Bournemouth goal celebration to a more solemnly reverential level?”
43 min: Tavernier whips a free-kick dangerously across the Milan goal and it nearly drops in the top corner with Torriani, the youngster, a mere spectator in goal.

42 min: Gannon-Doak with more good work down the right. He beats his man and bends a fine cross into the danger zone. Savage, on commentary, is purring his approval of some good old-fashioned wing play.

40 min: Truffert chases a ball down the left channel for Bournemouth. He does well to gather the ball and cut back inside the defender. Overall, the hosts look far superior to their opponents. Sharper in how they use the ball, quicker to press – you name it.
On the bench, Christian Pulisic and Luka Modric are pictured looking suitably ashen-faced.
Goal! 32 min - Bournemouth 2-0 Milan (Tavernier pen)
It’s there! Marcus Tavernier strokes in the second penalty of the night. Milan are all over the shop, down to 10, a callow 21-year-old keeper now in nets. This could be a cricket score!

30 min: The replacement goalkeeper, Lorenzo Torriani, comes on. But they haven’t taken anyone off! This is funny. Torriani runs off again. And they make a change: Omari Hutchinson is hooked by Amorim, who appears apologetic.

Maignan pushes Tyler Adams in the face at the resulting corner … and is immediately shown a red card! It’s being checked by the VAR. Astonishing scenes. Is the red card going to be confirmed? Is it a penalty? Will football ever be the same again?

The red card is confirmed. Maignan is asked to leave the field, having been loitering around for a while. Fikayo Tomori of Milan looks furious. Maignan wanders off, and we’ll have a new goalie in place for another penalty …
21 min: Kluivert gets another chance: this time, Milan try to play out from the back, but they fluff it up. It’s a good sight of goal but straight at the goalie, Mike Maignan.

articles.headline: Can the Valkyries come back against the Dream? What’s gone wrong for Golden State in the WNBA Finals
keyFacts: The Golden State Valkyries trail the Atlanta Dream 2-1 in the WNBA Finals after suffering back-to-back double-digit losses.
Valkyries players and head coach Natalie Nakase cited defensive lapses, poor composure, and execution issues as reasons for their recent struggles.
The Valkyries plan to focus on rest, review film, and prepare for Game 4 in their efforts to bounce back in the series.
body: ATLANTA — The Golden State Valkyries are not overreacting. At least that's what they said. They have to, or else the WNBA Finals series they trail 2-1 is as good as already lost.

The buzzwords in the organizational word cloud that once underscored their success are now in disarray. Gabby Williams described their defense as undisciplined after allowing 97 points — nearly 20 more than their postseason average — to the Atlanta Dream in Game 3. Tiffany Hayes wants more fight in their tank to best a team that she said "wanted it more." Veronica Burton voiced a bit of surprise that their composure has fallen short, allowing the Dream late surges to pull away.

Head coach Natalie Nakase, for a second straight game, questioned the delivery and understanding of a game plan built on all three. Ahead of Game 2, she said she "anticipated" a full four quarters. Then before Game 3, she promised their "best fight."
"Yeah, sometimes promises aren't kept," Nakase said on the heels of back-to-back double-digit losses.

Trailing 2-1 in an expanded best-of-seven series is not inherently a major problem. A comeback is doable. Of the 64 times a team went up 2-1 in the NBA Finals, 14 teams came back from the early deficit. Nakase experienced it first hand when, as an assistant with the Los Angeles Clippers in 2020, they collapsed despite a 3-1 series lead.

"It is a long series," center and three-time Las Vegas Aces champion Kiah Stokes told reporters on a Zoom call on Thursday. "I think we're still very positive. We know we can fix [it]. A lot of it is dealing with ourselves, so we just got to kind of look in the mirror first and then move forward."

The concern is more that the Valkyries have not looked anywhere close to themselves, can't currently use their record billion-dollar valuation to buy any desperately needed buckets and might be slogging through the rest of the series with an injury to their main scorer.

Williams came up limping holding her left knee after a Game 1 fourth-quarter collision with Dream point guard Jordin Canada. She said afterward it was a "long physical game, but I'm OK." Asked directly after Game 3 if her knee, which had a bag of ice on it, was OK, she said "yes."

The underappreciated forward proved early in the Valkyries' postseason run she can be and is an elite bucket-getter worth having the ball in the final minutes. She opened the series with an electric 26 points, despite shooting 36.4%. In the losses, she's been quiet, inefficient overall (8 of 33) and nearly nonexistent from the 3-point line (4 of 14).

The Valkyries have insisted the shots will start falling, that the looks are the ones they want. But when a team made it here on offense-optional mode anyway, facing a similarly elite defense winning the battle of styles by speeding one up and snatching possessions, can that be counted upon?

The Valkyries were 34.8% from the floor in Game 3, a number boosted merely by finding their stroke from range (12 of 30). Their scoring drought to start the game stood as the margin for much of the contest, until the Dream doubled their 7-point lead in the final three minutes of the third quarter with a 12-2 run.

It's a team of the collective built on the strength of, as Nakase said again on Thursday, it being "anyone's night." Yet it's been no one's lately. They took as many field goal attempts as Atlanta, but made 10 fewer baskets. They gave up 22 points off 17 turnovers, feeding directly into the Dream's grasp. They were slow defensively, while Atlanta finally cracked the series' offensive code after frustratingly low 30% shooting nights from all.
"You shoot, what, 49%? I mean, you win games," Dream leader Angel Reese said.
Certainly, these are things that could be fixed by the Valkyries returning to their principles and locking in with a sense of urgency they said they had, but hasn't always come across.

The series set up to be one decided at the margins, and some are less controllable. After the Dream took five more free throws in Game 1, a 68-64 Valkyries victory, they are winning the free throw battle by a significant mark of +16 in Game 2 and +12 in Game 3. Stokes' answer was clear: "Don't foul."
"We can't control what the refs call, but we can try to make it clear to not foul," Stokes said after Game 2. "But that's on us. We just can't be reaching and getting really dumb fouls."

The turnaround to Game 3 was tighter than originally scheduled. While typically teams would have a travel day and practice day before Game 3, the game was played two days after Game 2 to allow for it to be moved to State Farm Arena. Nakase said players' rest and recovery will be at the forefront of Thursday's schedule. Teams are scheduled to practice on Friday with an early 1 p.m. ET tip on Saturday. Game 5 is on Monday at Chase Center (8 p.m. ET, USA Network).

It gifts Nakase time to figure out what's truly behind the uncharacteristic play and what button she needs to press to fix it. She's a big believer in listening. In huddles, in the locker room, in crunch moments like these that can bring them closer. She's noticed them falling off a "fine line" of doing too much themselves versus trusting the balanced team approach that brought them to their first Finals in the franchise's second season.

After Game 3, her plan was to listen to them individually rather than in groups and go through various film sessions in line of individual, group, team. She mentioned directly that players might be confused by the game plan and that it was up to her to be more clear.

"[It's about] control what we can control and just make sure for us, me as a coach, is that I'm delivering a more efficient game plan," Nakase said on Thursday. "That's on me. I've got to come with a really aggressive game plan that the players all feel comfortable with."
Burton indicated on Thursday that players were aware and comfortable with what the coaching staff expected.
"At the end of the day, if we're not disciplined to it and to what we talk about doing, then we can't put so much on the coaches," Burton said.

To deliver on it correctly and consistently every possession is what creates champions. To this point, the Valkyries haven't leveled up. Their best option is to look ahead at the next opportunity to back up expectation.

articles.headline: UCLA vs. Michigan State prediction, pick, odds, spread: Bruins look to continue surprising unbeaten start
keyFacts: No. 9 UCLA will host Michigan State on Saturday in a Big Ten matchup featuring two programs led by first-year coaches.
UCLA enters the game with a 6-0 record under coach Bob Chesney but will play with backup quarterback Ty Dieffenbach following a season-ending injury to Nico Iamaleava.
Michigan State holds a 2-5 record and is seeking its first conference win under coach Pat Fitzgerald.
body: A pair of Big Ten programs heading in divergent directions under first-year coaches will square off Saturday, as No. 9 UCLA hosts Michigan State at 3:30 p.m. Eastern on CBS. The Bruins (6-0, 4-0 Big Ten) have emerged as a stunning success story under first-year coach Bob Chesney, while the Spartans (2-5, 0-4) are still trying to find their footing under new coach Pat Fitzgerald.

Across the Big Ten and SEC, UCLA is the last remaining undefeated team as the Bruins continue building a profile with eery similarities to the 2024 Indiana team. Chesney is just the second head coach in FBS history to start his tenure 6-0 for a team that was coming off a 9-loss season. The other was Curt Cignetti with the Hoosiers in 2024.

Both coaches came from James Madison and immediately ignited struggling Big Ten outfits. It's been a tougher road for Fitzgerald, the former longtime Northwestern coach who returned to the sideline this season after three years away from the college game. The Spartans' last two losses have come by a combined total of four points against Illinois and Northwestern.
Michigan State is now seeking to avoid starting 0-5 in Big Ten play in back-to-back seasons for the first time in program history as it heads west for its first road game against UCLA since 1974.
UCLA vs. Michigan State: Need to know

Turning to Dieffenbach: UCLA starting quarterback Nico Iamaleava suffered a season-ending knee injury in the Bruins' Week 6 win over Oregon, leaving the Bruins in the hands of Ty Dieffenbach. The Cal Poly transfer held his own in UCLA's 17-7 win over Wisconsin last week and profiles similarly to Iamaleava. At 6-foot-6, he can see over the defense, and he takes long strides as a runner. His 264 passing yards against the Badgers marked a season-high for UCLA's passing game.

Revitalizing the run: UCLA rushed for 200-plus yards in each game during its 4-0 start before getting slowed down in wins over Oregon and Wisconsin the past two weeks. The Bruins totaled just 140 yards on the ground against the Ducks and dipped to a season-low 120 against the Badgers. Wisconsin limited UCLA star Wayne Knight to 23 yards on 13 carries. If the Bruins are going to reach the full potential they flashed during the season's first half, getting the most out of Knight will be pivotal, especially now that UCLA is using its backup quarterback.

Playoff implications: UCLA has a 28.4% chance of making the College Football Playoff entering the game, according to the CBS Sports CFP Forecaster. That mark improves to 35.2% with a win but plummets to 11.4% with a loss. Because of their light schedule strength, the Bruins would be in grave danger of missing the playoff at 10-2. A 5-1 (or 6-0) finish will likely be required for this team to reach the 12-team field.

articles.headline: Rhode Island sues Meta over its approach to scam ads
keyFacts: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha filed a lawsuit against Meta alleging the company fails to prevent scam ads because they generate revenue.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone stated the company has removed over 159 million scam ads and criticized the attorney general for refusing to engage.
Rhode Island is the first state to take legal action against Meta over these specific scam ad allegations.
body: Rhode Island sues Meta over its approach to scam ads
It’s the first state to sue the social media company on these allegations.

Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha has filed a lawsuit against Meta over the company's handling of scam advertisements. The suit alleges that the social media business does not do enough to prevent fraudulent ads on its platforms. It further claims that Meta has not taken stronger action against those scams because they generate revenue for the company.

"For a company that engages so many Rhode Islanders and Americans, maintaining high standards for consumer safety should be of the utmost importance," Neronha said. "As alleged, Meta knowingly exposed vulnerable users to fraud and scams, and made enormous profits in doing so. When companies, big or small, take advantage of Rhode Island consumers, this Office will do everything within our authority to hold them to account."

In a statement to Reuters, which first reported on the state lawsuit, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the company has removed more than 159 million scam ads from its platforms. "The attorney general refused to engage with us on ways we protect Rhode Islanders from scams, and has instead hired an out-of-state private law firm to concoct a lawsuit that ignores the full range of actions we take to combat scams every day," Stone said.

The release from the AG's office says Rhode Island is the first state to take action over the alleged inaction, although it isn't the first time the social media company has been sued on this subject. The Consumer Federation of America filed a lawsuit in April and Santa Clara County in California did the same in May.

A 2025 report from Reuters found that scam advertisements across its networks could be providing billions of dollars for Meta, possibly as much as 10 percent of its revenue. The company has engaged in actions to shut down the bad actors behind some of those phony ads and sue the creators of other ones. It also added some user protections for suspicious messages earlier this year.

articles.headline: Brad Lander went olive picking in Israel. What he harvested was a campaign headline
keyFacts: Israeli forces briefly detained New York congressional candidate Brad Lander and activists during an olive harvest near Nahalin, according to Lander and police.
Israeli police said the group entered an unauthorized area without coordination, while Israel's Foreign Ministry called the event a political provocation.
Police stated that four foreign activists were transferred to the Population and Immigration Authority for hearings over online anti-Israel activity.
body: It was olive-harvest season in Judea and Samaria . It was also election season in New York . That cannot be separated from Brad Lander’s decision to leave the district he hopes to represent and join activists near Beitar Illit’s security fence.
Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District, was briefly detained Wednesday while accompanying Palestinian farmers near the village of Nahalin.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis & volunteers,” Lander posted. “We were simply harvesting olives.”

Taken alone, those words create the image Lander needed: Israeli forces descending upon peaceful farmers and rabbis for picking olives. That narrative unraveled through my conversation with Lt. Dean Elsdunne, international spokesman for the Israel Police, who supplied the missing sequence.

Elsdunne shared police statements saying the activists had arrived “without prior coordination” at an agricultural area near Beitar Illit’s security fence, where olive harvesting was prohibited without authorization. IDF and Border Police forces were then dispatched with officers from the Etzion Police Station.

The most revealing part of this story emerges only when the scattered pieces are placed together: an experienced group, no advance coordination, olives that were not yet ripe, an election less than two weeks away, and immediate condemnation from New York before the police account was considered. Most headlines captured the detention. Few examined the chain of choices that produced it.

Elsdunne said police were examining the incident with the Israel Defense Forces, the Foreign Affairs and Interior ministries, and authorities “with the aim of preventing friction, public disturbances, and incidents that could cause international damage.” That is the damage this episode produced.

I contacted T’ruah for comment, asking why it or its partners had not coordinated with the IDF in advance. This organized group had participated in similar visits before and should have known the procedures. T’ruah never responded.

The local farmers themselves acknowledged that the olives were not yet ripe, while making clear they would accept whatever assistance they could receive. The delegation could have coordinated a later visit when its assistance would have been more useful and less likely to create a security confrontation.
It did not.

Imagine the backlash if a pro-Israel candidate left the United States less than two weeks before an election for a politically charged appearance in Israel. Critics would question the candidate’s timing, judgment, and priorities. Brad Lander deserves exactly the same scrutiny.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry called the episode a “calculated political provocation.”
“This was not about harvesting olives,” it declared. “It was about harvesting headlines.” The ministry added: “Brad Lander came looking for a confrontation. Now he is pretending to be its victim.”

Elsdunne’s police update undercuts the suggestion that authorities indiscriminately imprisoned peaceful visitors. It said 32 activists were questioned and released with restrictions prohibiting their return to the area. The remaining 40 were released that afternoon after investigators found no grounds to hold them further.

Four foreign activists faced additional proceedings after police said their online anti-Israel activity had been identified, including expressions of support for organizations opposed to Israel. Those cases were transferred to the Population and Immigration Authority for hearings, according to the statement Elsdunne provided.

Lander, meanwhile, was released after authorities learned he was a congressional candidate. Others spent longer absorbing the consequences of a political performance that experienced organizers should have prevented.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani amplified Lander’s framing without qualification.
“Today Brad Lander, rabbis, and other New Yorkers accompanied Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest. For that, they were detained by the Israeli government,” Mamdani wrote.
“Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is,” he continued, while accusing Israel of committing “a horrific genocide against Palestinians.”
That was not an attempt to understand Elsdunne’s documented sequence. It was a political indictment delivered before the police account had been considered.

This is not the first time an American politician has turned an Israeli security response into political content. In July, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) claimed soldiers and settlers detained his delegation during a visit to Judea and Samaria. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said the embassy had not been notified.
“We would have said don’t go to restricted zone,” Huckabee wrote.

Once may be poor preparation. Repeating the formula looks like a strategy: enter a sensitive area without ensuring authorities have been notified, wait for security forces to respond, and portray that response as proof of Israeli oppression.
The performance is politically fraudulent. It removes the decisions that produced the confrontation and sells the response as the entire story.

These political stunts must stop. Israel and the IDF should not be used as campaign props by American politicians seeking attention or approval from their political base. Every edited video and context-free accusation strengthens a narrative in which Israel is presumed guilty before the facts are known. Jewish students, synagogues, businesses, and communities across America are left carrying the consequences.

Violence against Palestinian farmers or their property should be investigated and punished. Supporting Palestinian rights does not require erasing Israel’s security responsibilities or manufacturing confrontations.
BRAD LANDER THOUGHT HE WAS AN ALLY. THE MOB JUST SAW A JEW

Lander is running to represent New Yorkers in Congress . Voters should ask why, less than two weeks before Election Day, he was harvesting olives near Beitar Illit instead of addressing the people whose votes he is seeking.
The trees produced a crop. The confrontation produced footage, outrage, and political attention. The olives could wait. Lander’s campaign could not.

Ariella Noveck is a journalist and Washington Examiner opinion contributor specializing in antisemitism, Israel, and Middle East affairs, with extensive experience covering Jewish communities worldwide. Her work includes on-the-ground reporting, interviews with world leaders, and analysis of major geopolitical events. She can be followed on X and Instagram @AriellaNoveck.

articles.headline: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia
keyFacts: The Browser Company announced it will shut down the Arc browser on December 22, 2026, to focus engineering efforts on its AI-first browser, Dia.
The shutdown process includes stopping new Arc accounts immediately, removing AI features from Arc Search on November 23, and deactivating Arc on Mac and Windows by December 22.

Data will transfer to Dia, which will include equivalent features like profiles and optional vertical tabs, while CEO Josh Miller stated Arc cannot be open-sourced because it relies on proprietary technology powering Dia.
body: The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI.
“Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote.
“Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”

The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser.

On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store.

While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed, with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open-source.

But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK)—a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property.
“While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.”

For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.”
Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional.

The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company—which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025—conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “novelty tax” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.

articles.headline: The 2026 election could reshape healthcare
keyFacts: Democrats are prioritizing healthcare reform in the 2026 midterms amid widespread public concern over medical costs, according to the article.
Advocate Natalie Davis stated that the 2026 and 2028 elections will determine whether future healthcare reform succeeds or fails.
Democrats will likely advance healthcare legislation next year to establish policy priorities before 2028, the article stated.
body: New Yorkers march in support of universal healthcare this summer. | LightRocket via Getty Images
Americans are furious about the state of our healthcare system.

A recent KFF poll found 60 percent of US adults worry about the cost of medical care — more than gasoline, food and groceries, or their rent or mortgage. One in three Americans say they worry every day or almost every day about their ability to afford healthcare, per a new survey from the Pew Research Center . There seems to be a growing appetite for reform, too: More than 65 percent of Americans say they support the government spending more tax dollars to lower healthcare costs.

Democrats are trying to weaponize those frustrations against the Republicans who currently hold Congress and the White House. By a 2-to-1 margin, voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans on healthcare. That could mean single-payer Medicare-for-all or a new public insurance option or maybe something else. What all this energy leads to will depend on what happens in November. The candidates themselves are framing the stakes in those existential terms.
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter

Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here .

“Medicare for all is where we need to go,” Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Michigan Senate race whose support for the policy has been widely covered, said during an August interview with CNN. “And my hope is, both coming out of the 2026 midterms and then out of 2028, that we’re going to be on our way to a Senate majority to be able to get this done.”

Real change will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election and a new occupant in the White House. But this year’s midterms are still a make-or-break moment: The candidates who get elected this year, and how they shape the upcoming presidential primary debate and actions in Congress, will determine whether healthcare reform happens at all.
If you’re fed up with the state of American healthcare, and you want to see a change, you should show up for the midterms on Tuesday, November 3.
Big midterm wins can beget big healthcare wins

The classic pattern in American elections is that more voters go to the polls during presidential campaigns than during the midterm elections when only House and Senate seats are on the ballot. Turnout has started to tick up for the midterms in recent years, but it still trails behind presidential years. Midterms suffer from the perception that there’s not as much at stake if the White House is not on the line.
But that’s never been strictly true.

Midterm elections are extraordinarily important in shaping the future of policymaking, even if the payoff is delayed. They help determine both the character of the Congress that could eventually pass a major bill after the next presidential election, and the kind of ideas and policies that are going to be prioritized.

“Voters should see 2026 and 2028 as the elections that will guide the next big change in our healthcare system,” said Natalie Davis , CEO and co-founder of the advocacy group United States of Care, in a statement to Vox. “These elections will be how voters’ demands are heard — and will tell us whether the next real window for change will come with serious reforms or missed opportunity.”
A walk through the recent history of healthcare reform should help make the stakes of the 2026 elections clear.

In 2006, the national mood looked similar to what we’re seeing today. A very unpopular Republican president was in office, and the country had soured on his agenda. George W. Bush’s foreign wars and his misguided attempt to overhaul Social Security gave Democrats an opportunity to win big in the 2006 midterms — and they did. Dems won more than 30 seats and secured a comfortable majority in the House . In the Senate , they won six seats and narrowly took control of that chamber too.

It was a resounding rejection of the Bush administration, and it set up the next decade of Democratic policymaking. At the highest level, the midterms gave energy to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, united as they were around their opposition to the Iraq War, and that energy carried over to the presidential primary. Barack Obama defeated Hillary Clinton and won the presidency, springboarding off of the excitement that started with the 2006 elections.

Dems’ success in the midterms also helped put lowering healthcare costs at the forefront of the Democratic agenda. That encouraged both Obama and Clinton to develop detailed healthcare policy proposals during their primary campaigns and ultimately set the stage for the Democrats to pursue the Affordable Care Act once they had full control of the government in 2009.

And then there is the literal size of the congressional majorities that parties need to pass their agenda. Voters may not spend much time thinking about whip counts, but one or two elections in a midterm year can ultimately decide the fate of the next president’s agenda.

Part of the reason Democrats were able to pass the ACA was that they built on their huge wins in 2006 with more wins in 2008 and held massive congressional majorities once Obama was sworn in. And once the debate over healthcare reform really got started, they needed every single vote. It was especially important in the Senate: Democrats had exactly 60 votes in 2009. That meant if all of them united together, they could pass filibuster-proof legislation — so long as nobody defected. That was only possible because in 2006 Mark Pryor won a Senate seat in Arkansas, Sherrod Brown triumphed in a Senate race in Ohio, and Jon Tester beat an incumbent Republican in Montana.

Without those wins in 2006, the Democratic legislative agenda in 2009 would probably have looked different. They might’ve had to pursue a more limited healthcare reform plan; maybe the ACA wouldn’t have passed at all.
What kind of Democrats will be on the rise in 2028?

The 2006 midterms both created the opportunity for the ACA — and set the limits on what the legislation could actually achieve. Democrats had that 60-seat Senate majority, but within it were many more moderate members. Policies like the public option (which would have authorized the government to create its own health insurance plan to sell alongside private insurance) couldn’t get sufficient support. That is the dilemma of policymaking: You need those swing-seat members to win, which often means tacking to the center, but you also can’t pass anything they won’t get on board with.
Nevertheless, that is a good kind of political problem to have, one which Democrats would be thrilled to face in January 2029. All of which brings us to 2026. What are we going to do now?

It all starts with the vote count. Most projections expect the Democrats to win between 10 and 20 House seats. But the difference between 10 and 20 could be substantial. The cushier the majority, the further you can push the policy agenda. More than 30 House Democrats actually voted against the ACA, but they could still narrowly pass the bill because of the huge majority that they had started building in 2006.

If you live in one of the districts — like Arizona’s Sixth or Colorado’s Eighth or Florida’s 22nd, to name just a couple of the 21 toss-up races identified by the Cook Political Report this year — that forecasters say is competitive this year, you could have an outsized say in what the future of policymaking looks like. But even in safe districts, you should vote: Elections are the most reliable way we have to gauge public opinion, and strong victories for the candidates who prioritize healthcare send a message.

The same goes for the Senate. If Democrats sweep all of the competitive races , they could have up to 55 seats in the Senate in 2027 — with a chance to build on it in 2028. If you are a voter in Kansas, Michigan, Ohio, Texas, Alaska, Maine, New Hampshire, or Iowa, your ballot carries extra weight for the next steps in US healthcare reform. If the Democrats can reach 60 votes again in 2029, they would have much more flexibility about what to pass. Even if they fall short of that magic number, the more of a cushion they have above 50, the more likely that their Senate leaders can find support for altering Senate rules for the filibuster and get an ambitious bill approved.
How you can get involved this election
If there is ever going to be a path to a true healthcare overhaul, it starts with this year’s elections. If you want to see a change, you can vote — and you can do more than that.
Talk to your neighbors.
Phone bank for candidates you believe in.
You can even sign up to drive people to the polls on Election Day.

The results of this year’s midterms will also set the terms of the debate among Democrats. We are likely to see “show” bills advanced by Dems next year that may have no chance of being signed by President Donald Trump, but that will give us a sense of what kind of policies the party wants to pursue and how much support there is for them. Believe it or not, the first Medicare prescription drug negotiations bill passed the House in 2007 after Democrats’ big wins in 2006 — even though the policy didn’t become law for another 15 years . The broader public may not pay much attention to this kind of doomed-to-fail legislation, but it is often a window into the future.

“One challenge for Democrats is finding the next big health care idea beyond the Affordable Care Act that will resonate with voters and respond to their affordability concerns,” said Larry Levitt , executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “One big difference between now and 2006 is that back then there was already a lot of coalescing around ideas that ultimately led to the ACA. All the major Democratic candidates for president in 2008 supported something like that. I’m not sure that’s true now, at least not yet.”

Democrats are already aligning on a wide range of healthcare ideas, from reviving the public option to free primary care to the full-blown Medicare-for-all supported by progressive candidates, some of whom are in competitive elections. If El-Sayed wins the Senate race in Michigan, for example, that could supercharge a debate around Medicare-for-all. It could also provide momentum to any progressives who run for president — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to name one obvious example — and decide to make Medicare-for-all a pillar of their platform.

But if El-Sayed and other progressives were to fall short, that could make Democrats more timid about being ambitious in the 2028 campaign and afterward. Still, he’s far from the only candidate in a crucial race to put their support behind Medicare-for-all. There is Randy Villegas in an important California House race. Troy Jackson has bet on it as part of his bid to topple Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. All of these races will send a signal to the party about what the public wants and is willing to turn out for.

In some ways, winning elections is the easy part. Legislating is hard, and any eventual healthcare law will surely involve compromises and unexpected surprises. Who knows what will be happening in the world in 2029?

“The bottom line is: 2026 is a healthcare election,” the leaders of the advocacy group Protect Our Care wrote in a campaign memo this month. “After November, it’s up to Democrats to keep up the fight to deliver relief to families and make healthcare affordable and accessible for every American .”

articles.headline: What cost England in epic as 'box office' Brook's 'genius' goes to waste?
keyFacts: Sri Lanka successfully chased a target of 430 runs to beat England in an ODI tri-series match in Rawalpindi.
Harry Brook scored a record-breaking double century for England from 114 balls, which he stated had no value because they lost.
Pundit Nasser Hussain said England's bowling struggles, specifically bowling too short and failing to take middle-overs wickets, caused the defeat.
body: What cost England in ODI run-fest vs Sri Lanka as Harry Brook's 'genius' double century has 'no value whatsoever'?

Harry Brook wows Sky pundits Nasser Hussain and Mark Butcher with record-breaking ODI double ton from 114 balls but England end up on losing side after bowling too short and lack of middle-overs wickets; Sam Curran goes at 11.44 runs an over in expensive outing
Thursday 22 October 2026 20:35, UK
At the halfway stage, most people would have given Sri Lanka no chance.
The ask was a herculean 430, second only to the 438-9 South Africa peeled off versus Australia in Johannesburg in 2006 when it came to successful ODI run chases.
But on a day when South Africa beat Australia once again - this time in a one-sided Test match in Gqeberha - Sri Lanka stunned England in a Rawalpindi run-fest.

That meant Harry Brook's astonishing 202 from 116 balls, during which he reached 200 from 114 deliveries to set a new record for the fastest ODI double ton, came in vain.
So where exactly did things go wrong for England?
How did England lose that game?

Not with the batting, obviously, as Brook's sizzling knock - the highest for England in a men's ODI, eclipsing the 182 Ben Stokes scored against New Zealand in 2023 - was backed up by half-centuries from Tom Banton, Joe Root and Will Jacks.

The bowling was the issue with Sri Lanka rallying from 24-2 once Kamindu Mendis had been bowled by a beauty from Josh Tongue and captain Kusal Mendis was run out backing up without facing a ball after Gus Atkinson tipped on to the non-striker's stumps.

Sky Sports' Nasser Hussain noted how England overcompensated from bowling too full during their 87-run defeat to Pakistan at the same venue on Tuesday by dropping too short, particularly to Pavan Rathnayake, who top-scored with 130 from 106 balls.

The former England captain also lamented his country's long-standing issue of middle-overs wickets, with only one taken between Kusal's run out in the fifth over and Rathnayake holing out off the expensive Sam Curran at long-on in the 41st.
Rathnayake put on 166 with Avishka Fernando for the third wicket and then 133 with the wisely-promoted Dasun Shanaka for the fourth - both of his team-mates made 97.
Hussain: Lack of middle-order wickets a concern for England
Hussain said of the wicketless woes: "It comes from that middle period where England, historically, over the last two or three years, have struggled to take wickets.

"That is even with Adil Rashid, who did not play in this game, at his best, so that is something they need to solve, a box they need to tick. Getting back Jofra Archer, rested for this series, will help and add a bit of firepower.
"Maybe Adil has come off his best but today showed the need for Archer, and Rashid being back to his best. We all big up Adil but he has just dropped off, maybe because of injuries."
Former Sri Lanka batter and Hussain's fellow Sky Sports pundit Kumar Sangakkara said: "England needed an all-out push to take wickets when they had Sri Lanka 24-2. You have 429 on the board.

"Have set plays, try to bowl the bumpers, fielders set for catches - of if you want to restrict because conditions are not suitable for wickets, then go to death bowling early, try to cut off the boundaries.
"The only way they were going to lose the game was by the boundary count rising. If you are a fast bowler, you stop the fours with fields set and the sixes by executing the best deliveries.
"Still, England need to give credit to an incredible batting performance from Sri Lanka."
Sri Lanka get over the line after 'marathon'
That point about Sri Lanka is an important one from Sangakkara.

For as loose as England were with the ball - Curran, in just his second game since The Hundred in August due to a groin injury, struggled to land his moon balls and yorkers and was flogged for 103 runs from his nine overs - Sri Lanka were superb.

They showed grit after slipping two down early, then the ability to adapt by pushing Shanaka up the order - he smoked eight sixes in his 50-ball 97 - and when late wickets had seen Sri Lanka wobble a bit, Janith Liyanage fired under pressure with an unbeaten 61.

Liyanage crunched two fours and a six across three balls off Curran to trim the ask to 29 from 21 deliveries and then spanked the winning six with one ball to spare after Tongue has taken two wickets in two deliveries earlier in the final over.
Hussain added: "Sri Lanka had to be pretty much perfect for 50 overs and they were. There were lads in there who played pretty much the perfect innings.
"It was like running a marathon for Sri Lanka - they saw that last bit and started to stumble when they needed to be calm.
"So Liyanage in the end - that was incredibly special. You looked at his body language, it was like, 'leave it to me, lads' - he was calm, composed and belted it down the ground.
"It was a perfect, historic chase and brilliant for Sri Lanka. They are such a talented, passionate cricketing nation. They needed a day like today and they got one."
Why Brook said his double hundred 'does not matter'
Brook had spoken earlier in the week about wishing there was a match-winning column in players' stats.
If that was part of cricket, then for a long time in Rawalpindi on Thursday it looked like Brook's would have a big fat tick in it.
In the end, though, the Yorkshireman insisted that his individual heroics "didn't matter."

Brook, whose innings featured 21 fours and 10 sixes said: "I always say I want to make match-winning contributions, have a match-winning impact. Unfortunately I've got 200 and it's not been match-winning. In my eyes, it doesn't matter. It had no value whatsoever."

Still, Hussain and Sky Sports colleague Mark Butcher enthused over the England captain, with Hussain calling him the best male multi-format batter in the world and saying his presence makes the team contenders at next year's 50-over World Cup in Africa.
The pundit added: "Every shot selection he made was spot on - it had to be to score 200 that quickly. He has been touched by genius ever since we have seen him.
"The biggest area of growth for this ODI team is if Brook can convert his Test and T20 form into this format. He did that, it was magical.
Butcher said: "Sometimes your breath is taken away with Brook and you don't quite have the words to describe what you are watching.
"Such is his precision and the way he can uses the pace on the ball, he can pretty much manoeuvre it wherever he likes. Then he will fly out of the crease and hit you for six.
"He has such balance, his hands are so good, the control of the bat face is as good as anybody I have seen. He can play a shot for pretty much every delivery. He is absolutely box office."
Now, if England could just get the bowling sorted…
