articles.headline: Aipac halts candidate endorsements amid US backlash against Israel
keyFacts: Aipac announced that it will stop endorsing political candidates and end direct financial contributions to them.
Critics said the policy change reflects growing political backlash against Israel that made Aipac's public support a liability for candidates.
Aipac pledged to continue financing pro-Israel candidates using its super PAC, United Democracy Project, and individual member donations.
body: When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in the US, announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates or make direct contributions to them, its many critics were quick to hail the development as Aipac’s admission of how toxic its brand had become.

The announcement marked a significant reversal that underscored just how profoundly US public opinion of Israel has shifted over the latest war in Gaza, and how political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability.

But Aipac, which only launched its political action committee and started endorsing candidates three cycles ago, is hardly getting out of US elections. It pledged to maintain the work of its deep-pocketed super pac, United Democracy Project, and to continue to funnel millions of dollars to prop up pro-Israel candidates through individual donors and Aipac members. The shift in strategy was a sign it was adapting to a changing political landscape, not that it was giving up its efforts to shape it.

“Historically, AIPAC sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover – if you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn’t even bother to fight you,” the political analyst Trita Parsi wrote. “Rather than invincibility, AIPAC’s name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn’t want its own name on its political donations.”

Aipac did not respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Aipac, which normally backs Democrats, was planning to give as much as $9m to a Pac supporting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The group had already spent $32m seeking to defeat El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, in the primaries.

But the announcement that it would stop directly backing candidates going forward was seen as tacit recognition that Aipac’s open support risked hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them.

“Through this shift, AIPAC openly admitted that their brand has become toxic in the political world,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, one of Aipac’s most vocal critics, told the Guardian. “Fewer and fewer candidates are willing to be publicly affiliated with this extremist, warmongering group. This is a clear signal: being pro-genocide is bad politics and bad policy.”

In a letter from Aipac to members first reported on by Jewish Insider, the group’s leadership seemed to acknowledge that its once formidable power in US elections had suffered as more candidates openly distanced themselves from Israel, and from the group itself. In the letter, they noted that the 2026 election was “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory” for the group and predicted that the “challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead.”

“To win the fight for the future of the country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation,” they wrote. “The only tactic we’re married to is the most effective one.”

While Aipac boasted that it helped 290 candidates this election cycle, leading to the defeat of 29 candidates it described as “anti-Israel”, the group has also suffered major blows – including in Michigan and New Jersey. More than a dozen candidates who took Aipac contributions in the past have since publicly distanced themselves from the group, and New York’s rep Pat Ryan announced last week that he would return nearly $250,000 from the group, the latest of several elected officials to return Aipac funds or say they would turn it down.

Dion Nissenbaum, a journalist whose documentary on Aipac was published this week, featuring interviews with former Aipac insiders, told the Guardian that the announcement appeared to be the “first real admission from Aipac that their campaign strategy has backfired”.
Still, he warned, “if Aipac’s super PAC – the main source of its campaign donations – is going to keep operating, it may be an attempt to reinvent itself without ceding the battlefield.”

Tuesday’s announcement would change little in practice, those who have monitored Aipac’s political funding say. An Aipac spokesperson told Jewish Insider that Aipac members had contributed over $90m to candidates this election cycle – far more than the $3m in donations the group contributed directly through its Pac.
“This is not new,” Hady Amr, a former secretary for Israeli and Palestinian affairs with the US state department, noted. “This is Aipac going back to their tried and true approach.”

Groups like TrackAipac and initiatives like the Reject Aipac campaign, that have in recent years played a growing role in calling out candidates over their ties to the group, are already attuned to the varied avenues through which the pro-Israel lobby funnelled contribution to candidates, some more visible than others.

“[Aipac] has already been experimenting with ways to make their support more untraceable,” said Hamid Bendaas of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, one of the groups behind the Reject Aipac campaign. By dropping endorsements and direct contributions, Aipac was giving up one tool available to lobby organizations to signal to politically-aligned donors who may not be active members which candidates to back. Aipac had calculated that approach was more risky than worth it, he added, but it had plenty of other tools available.

“It’s akin to an animal that chews its leg off to get out of a bear trap. It’s a last resort choice to survive and stay relevant, which they will on both counts,” Bendaas added. “Aipac is going to continue influencing elections. If you’re someone who wants Aipac out of politics entirely, this is not that.

“We know they’re going to continue driving tens of millions of dollars into our elections to support Israel’s atrocities,” echoed Miller, of JVP. “And we will continue to fight to fully get them, and their dirty money, out of our politics and out of Congress.”

articles.headline: GTA 6’s New TV Trailer Is A Bit Different, See It For Yourself
keyFacts: Fans discovered that new GTA 6 television commercials feature minor edits, including longer airplane and car scenes and the removal of the Xbox logo.
The 30-second TV spot removes shower scenes featuring Jason and Lucia, while a 90-second version includes them.
GTA 6 is scheduled to launch on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.
body: GTA 6 's marketing push is ramping up substantially, and that includes with TV commercials. Eagled-eyes fans have discovered that the new GTA 6 TV spots actually contain some extended sequences, but just barely.

For starters, a 30-second TV spot cuts out the steamy shower scenes with Jason and Lucia from the launch trailer . While the shower scenes are gone in this edit, the new TV spot has a slightly longer shots of an airplane sequence and another with Jason and Lucia standing next to their car.

Jason playfully nudges Lucia, and in the TV spot, she nearly topples to the ground. The Xbox logo was also removed, presumably due to Rockstar's reported promotional deal with Sony. You can check out the comparison below ( via IGN ).
https://twitter.com/GTAVI_Countdown/status/2112897438885245268

A 90-second version, meanwhile, includes the shower scenes, along with the slightly longer sequences seen in the 30-second version. If you saw these TV spots recently, you might not have even noticed any of these changes, but GTA 6 fan accounts are extremely dedicated and never miss anything.
https://twitter.com/mnm345x/status/2113001090245664971

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and, yes, Xbox Series X|S, even though the TV ads for the game don't tell you that. Rockstar's marketing push for the game also includes real-life Burger Shot and Cluckin' Bell restaurants where you can buy GTA-branded food .

In other GTA 6 news, it was recently reported that preorders are pacing significantly ahead of any other big AAA game of the past five years . Obviously that's no surprise, given GTA 6 is expected to be the biggest game release ever, and it could generate $2 billion before it even launches.

articles.headline: Elon Musk opens wallet to aid NY Rep. Mike Lawler’s tough re-election bid
keyFacts: Elon Musk’s America Super PAC spent $600,000 to support Representative Mike Lawler’s re-election bid, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Political watchdogs have rated the close congressional race between incumbent Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley as a toss-up.
Filings indicate Musk will spend over one million dollars in the campaign’s final days to bolster Lawler and oppose Conley.
body: Elon Musk’s self-financed America Super PAC dumped $600,000 to back Lawler in recent days as the two-term Hudson Valley congressman faces a tough challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in next month’s midterms, Federal Elections Commission filings show.
It’s a strong indication that Musk, the owner of SpaceX, Tesla and X Corp., will spend more than a million dollars in the campaign’s final days to bolster Lawler and slam Conley.
The Musk spending so far covers contracts to StoryTellers LLC for printing, postage and other messaging supporting Lawler and opposing Conley, the FEC filings, first reported by Gothamist, said.
“It’s no surprise that Elon Musk has spent millions to keep his puppet Mike Lawler in office,” said Conley campaign spokesperson Maddy Rosen.

“Musk is the operator of the largest data center in the world, and Lawler cast the deciding vote to give data center operators $80 billion in tax breaks, while voting to ban states from regulating data centers and AI operations. As always, when it comes to Mike Lawler’s disastrous record, just follow the money.”

Lawler campaign spokesperson Ciro Riccardi responded, “By law, Lawler for Congress can’t coordinate with super PACs, and we have no say over what America PAC or any other outside group spends in this race.”

“Meanwhile, Cait Conley calls super PAC money ‘dark money,’ yet 27 outside groups, including a teachers’ union super PAC, VoteVets, and the League of Conservation Voters, have spent nearly $6.5 million to elect her. She even formed her own joint committee with House Majority PAC, a Washington super PAC, which has put millions into TV ads for her,” Riccardi said. “That’s hypocrisy.”

Another billionaire mogul, former three-term New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg, is opening his wallet and spending $80 million to help Democrats re-take the House and Senate and win other races in the Nov. 3 elections.
Super PACs affiliated with President Trump, including MAGA Inc., could end up spending upwards of $400 million to help Republicans.

Lawler, a former state assemblyman, is seeking a third-term to rep the district, which covers Westchester County from the White Plains border as far north as Hopewell Junction as well as Rockland, Putnam and Dutchess Counties.
Independent and internal party polls show the Lawler-Conley race is close and could be a nail-biter. Most political watchdogs have rated the race a toss-up.

Super PACS are independent expenditure groups that can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to influence campaigns, unlike candidates’ campaign committees that face limits on how much can be raised from individual donors under federal law.

articles.headline: Eddie Howe emerges as new favourite for Man United job as Michael Carrick’s authority diminishes
keyFacts: Manchester United technical director Jason Wilcox favours Eddie Howe as a replacement if manager Michael Carrick is sacked.
talkSPORT understands Carrick faces pressure following a 4-1 defeat to Como and public criticism from captain Bruno Fernandes.
Carrick is expected to manage Manchester United for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth while club leaders consider their options.
body: Manchester United technical director Jason Wilcox is leaning towards appointing Eddie Howe if Michael Carrick is sacked, talkSPORT understands.
Carrick faces an uphill battle to save his job in the wake of Wednesday’s humiliating 4-1 defeat at Como after which captain Bruno Fernandes rounded on his manager.
Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick’s tactics against Como AFP
Carrick is set to be in charge for Sunday’s Premier League home clash with Bournemouth as the United hierarchy contemplate their options moving forward.
Who are the contenders to replace Michael Carrick if he’s sacked?
As exclusively revealed by talkSPORT, former Germany and Bayern Munich chief Julian Nagelsmann has already been sounded out over his interest in taking charge at Old Trafford.
Nagelsmann is the standout option in the eyes of head of recruitment Christopher Vivell.
But Wilcox’s opinion is likely to hold more weight in the eyes of Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family.
Wilcox is believed to prefer Howe due to his experience in the Premier League even though he rallied against appointing him when Dan Ashworth put him forward prior to Ruben Amorim’s arrival.
Aston Villa boss Unai Emery also fits Wilcox’s criteria but would be expensive to prise away even if he wanted the job.
talkSPORT understands Fabian Hurzeler, another admired by Wilcox, would not leave Brighton for United at this time .
Antonio Conte has put himself forward to replace Carrick but that looks unlikely having been previously overlooked due to his fiery nature.
Bruno Fernandes set to avoid punishment for post-match outburst
In another ominous sign for Carrick, United do not plan to punish captain Fernandes for his incredible outburst.
There is a fear in the boardroom that the 2008 Champions League winner is losing the faith of the dressing room after overseeing United’s worst start to a season in 40 years.
Carrick has endured a torrid time since becoming United’s permanent manager Getty
Howe has been out of work since leaving Newcastle by mutual consent in the summer.
While he is not desperate to return to the dugout quickly the feeling is he would be interested if the United vacancy came his way.
At Newcastle, Howe ended the club’s 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when he led them to EFL Cup glory in 2025.
Howe also oversaw Newcastle’s return to the Champions League in 2023, 20 years after they were last in the competition.
The Magpies repeated the feat at the end of the 2024/25 campaign.
Howe’s final season at the helm ended with Newcastle finishing 12th, their lowest placing throughout his tenure at the club.

articles.headline: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
keyFacts: SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger.
Elon Musk stated on a SpaceX earnings call that combining the companies would help develop superintelligence software.
Sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg there is a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027.
body: Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.

The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”

If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.

Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.

At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.

As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder

SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.

Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement

SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.

On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger

Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.

Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money

Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”

Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.

Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:

It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.

It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?

The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”

Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”

At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout

Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.

Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.

What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.

What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.

Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.

So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

articles.headline: Breaking Down The Leaked Mass Effect 5 Trailer
keyFacts: EA shut down BioWare, which canceled their Mass Effect project known from a leaked trailer as Mass Effect: Universe.
The leaked trailer revealed a new human protagonist, repaired Mass Relays, and the return of the character Liara T'Soni.
It remains unclear if more details about the canceled game will emerge unless EA sells the intellectual property.
body: BioWare was shut down yesterday by EA, bringing a sudden end to a studio whose legacy of legendary role-playing games stretches back nearly 30 years. This meant that the studioâs Mass Effect project, being developed by a relative skeleton crew after a downsizing in January of 2025, was canceled, and fans likely wonât get the chance to return to the beloved science-fiction universe unless EA sells the IP. However, we got a new look at what the team was working on thanks to a leaked trailer, revealing that the game was going to be called Mass Effect: Universe.

The trailer is short, but thereâs a lot to extrapolate in the two minutes we see. We can also make some educated guesses based on the years of teases BioWare put out before EA shuttered the studio. So letâs try to make heads or tails of it all.
Where is this bar?

The trailer starts with an outside shot of a bar, and we can see a giant skyscraper outside that doesnât look quite like anything weâve seen before. It perhaps most closely resembles architecture seen in London after it gets rebuilt post-war in Mass Effect 3âs Extended Cut. Thereâs a pretty big mix of alien races here. We see Salarians, Turians, Volus, Asari, Quarians, Krogan, even a Drell or two. Part of me would be surprised if this was supposed to be on Earth considering just how diverse the barâs clientele is, but given that Universe was supposedly meant to take place hundreds of years after the original trilogy and Earth was the final battle ground of the Reaper War in ME3, maybe our planet became more of a tourist attraction. Or this could be somewhere the series has never taken us before, which is probably the more likely explanation.
We meet the third Mass Effect protagonist

While previous teases for the game that would have been Mass Effect: Universe implied it would somehow bridge the gap between the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies, most figured that we wouldnât have been playing as Andromeda protagonist Pathfinder Ryder. A loud and annoying contingent of fans wanted BioWare to bring back original trilogy hero Commander Shepard despite most of Mass Effect 3âs endings resulting in their death, as well as BioWareâs previous teases implying this game would take place closer to the events of Mass Effect: Andromeda. Thankfully, it looks like BioWare had no intention of bringing Shepard back.

Instead, we would have been playing as someone who seems like a kind of galactic James Bondâtype. An Asari approaches him and says that he looks like heâs military. He says he isnât anymore, and we get a flashback to his time fighting in the human Alliance military. He and his squad have a firefight against a group of Krogan. Last yearâs N7 Day teaser revealed that there were plans to feature some kind of Krogan civil war in the story, but itâs unclear if this is part of that conflict. Was this new guyâs squad intercepting some kind of Krogan mission, or were the big scary aliens just a formidable foe to show our new hero fighting off big baddies? Whatever the case, heâs out of that line of work. Too many fires to put out.
The Mass Relays have been repaired

Now that heâs no longer with the Alliance, heâs entered a ânew line of work.â Heâs still traveling throughout the galaxy, though, and is using the Mass Relay transit network to do it. Notably, these were all destroyed at the end of Mass Effect 3, though the Extended Cut DLC made a big hoopla about how that gutwrenching, galaxy-altering choice could be patched up, no big deal.Â
Manning a new ship with a new crew

We see a few shots of what would have been the new ship, and it looks a lot smaller than the Normandy from the trilogy or Tempest from Andromeda. Inside, we see our space-faring not-Bond talking with some crew members, including a human and Krogan, and looking at a galaxy map of the Milky Way. Itâs unclear if these would have been party members or part of the shipâs crew.Â
Wait, is that Illium?

Though the previous teasers imply that the Andromeda galaxy would play a part in the story, it does look like the majority of the game would have taken place in humanityâs home galaxy. One place we see our hero touch down looks an awful lot like Illium, a planet primarily occupied by the Asari that players visit frequently in Mass Effect 2.Â
Secret agent man

Though Shepard dabbled in some secret-agent hijinks over the course of the trilogy, it looks like Universe would have leaned into them more heavily, being primarily made up of espionage and more intimate firefights. We see our trench coatâwearing protagonist spying on people arriving on the planet that may or may not be Illium, getting into hand-to-hand scraps, and wielding both biotic abilities and tech skills to take down his enemies. He even scans a Salarianâs skull like heâs hacking into their systems for some kind of intel.Â
Love is in the air

Every Mass Effect game has love and sex in it, and Universe would have been no exception. We see a few shots of the new guy with someone who likely would have been one of his potential love interests. In one, he walks arm-in-arm with a woman into some kind of event; in the next, theyâre doing the horizontal tango in low lighting.Â
â¦Alright, what the hell is that?

Next, we see a party made up of the main character, a Krogan, and a Quarian teammate finding some kind of almost squid-like creature? My brain immediately goes to it being related to the Reapers or the Leviathan, as those are the most notable cephalopods in the franchise, though it looks like it has almost human-like skin. Whatever it is, it appears to be in some kind of stasis. The Quarian starts to scan it, but the only real information we can see from his screen is that this thing is in critical condition.
The queen has arrived

After a few more mood shots of the ship flying through a snowy area and trench coat boy getting into some more close-quarters combat, weâre back at the bar where the Asari whispers into our heroâs ear and threatens him. Her goons are ready to rough him up, until one of the bar patrons interrupts. Itâs none other than the Asari Liara TâSoni, the only party member from the previous games that had been confirmed to return in Universeâs original teasers. Then, a bar fight breaks out, and the new guy starts rocking the shit out of everyone in the bar. We even get a quick shot of Liara tossing some folks with her biotics, but the action is cut short and we see the title card.

As the trailer says at the beginning, Universe definitely looks like itâs still in an early concept phase to some extent, as the action doesnât look quite as polished in some places as it does in others. Still, if BioWare hadnât been shuttered and weâd seen it as intended, there would have been a lot of questions, such as how the Andromeda galaxy factors into all this considering that the 2023 teaser implied someone from the Milky Way would be answering a distress call from there. Hopefully, whether it be through more leaks or through developers being allowed to talk about what theyâre working on, weâll hear and see more about Mass Effect: Universe down the line. articles.headline: Meet the 2026 winner of Nikon's Small World photomicrography contest
keyFacts: German photographer Ole Bielfeldt won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with an image of ink droplets from an inkjet printer.
Bielfeldt developed his photography skills during the COVID-19 lockdown using an old microscope and custom-built tools.
To capture the fast-moving ink drops, Bielfeldt modified a printer and used a flash in a dark room instead of relying on the camera shutter.
body: A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.

Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying , his photography and videography brand.

It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.

articles.headline: Microsoft helped shut down an “App Store” for criminals linked to over a billion malicious messages
keyFacts: Microsoft announced a successful operation with the Japanese National Police Agency to disrupt cybercrime app stores.
The YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man targeted organizations in over 150 countries and sent over one billion malicious messages.
Microsoft stated that it has seized, blocked, or redirected domains associated with the YAM, CoGUI, and Iron Man infrastructure.
body: - Microsoft collaborated with the Japanese National Police Agency to tackle Chinese-language cybercrime “app stores”
- The YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man have targeted people in more than 150 countries
- Microsoft is working with law enforcement agencies worldwide to take down illegal operations that target businesses and individuals

Microsoft has announced a successful operation with the Japanese National Police Agency in which a collection of cybercrime app stores were disrupted. Investigating fraudulent, scam messages targeting Japanese businesses and citizens, the operation uncovered a multi-faceted criminal marketplace, with three key elements.

The YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man had targeted 75,000 organizations across more than 150 countries worldwide, sent over one billion malicious communications promoting scams, and generated millions of dollars for the criminals behind them. Furthermore, 750 million messages were aimed at Microsoft’s own customers.
Alongside the Japanese authorities, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, Resecurity, and TRM Labs were also involved in the operation.
Impersonation templates

Exploring the cybercrime ecosystem targeting Japanese businesses, investigators found the trio of the YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man. Investigators found these provided a route into a cybercrime ecosystem for cybercriminals.

The environment was providing criminals with pre-fabricated fake websites and messages, designed to be used to fool targets into thinking they were interacting with the genuine article. Amazon was among the faked sites, on sale so scammers could simply host convincing pages to steal login and payment credentials, without any need to hire their own coder. Other spoofs on sale included government agencies, financial institutions, and other well-known companies.

Security filtering software was initially unable to handle the CoGUI phishing-as-a-service (Phaas) framework as it employed some sophisticated methods to avoid detection, including browser fingerprinting and geofencing.

What is interesting to note is the role these facilities played for the distribution of cybercrime assets. CoGUI was apparently targeting Japan and US victims, but during the course of the investigation, was replaced by a new service, Iron Man.

The YAM Store

While all three components were already known to Microsoft and the authorities, it took a concerted effort to infiltrate the network of cybercriminals using the services. They were hosted in a wholly Chinese-language environment, requiring native-speakers to be added to the investigating team, and gain access to the underground cybercrime marketplace known as the YAM Store.

Microsoft assigned a tracking number Storm-3119 to the marketplace, which it describes as an “Initial Access Broker.” It was set up to provide its customers with “compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google.”

While it may be expected for compromised software to be on the radar of its publishers, the creator(s) of the YAM Store had a workaround. It was able to keep its inventory fresh by using automation. This identified “expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections.”
Microsoft has seized domains associated with the YAM/CoGUI/Iron Man infrastructure, and either blocked or redirected them.

articles.headline: Supreme Court justice turns on her own court with dire warning about American democracy
keyFacts: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan warned that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing American democracy.
Kagan argued that decisions on gerrymandering and campaign finance polarized the country and harmed the Supreme Court's legitimacy.
The Supreme Court is expected to rule on major cases concerning gun rights and state election laws during its current term.
body: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan made the case that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing democracy, suggesting that it isn't working "as well as it should."
The remarks from the liberal justice came during a closed discussion before faculty and students at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.

The discussion between Kagan and law professor Joel Alicea Alicia, who previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito, comes just weeks after the Supreme Court began its new term, during which it's expected to rule in major cases that will determine the scope of gun rights and state election integrity laws, among other issues.

The conversation also comes less than two weeks before the midterm elections as President Donald Trump and Republican state lawmakers have pushed for new congressional maps drawn to favor Republicans and bolster their chances of maintaining control of the House. Democratic-led states have responded by redrawing their own maps, fueling ongoing lawsuits and court battles.
SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE

Kagan pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2019 ruling in Rucho v. Common Cause , in which she dissented, as the beginning of a "race to the bottom." She argued that the decision, which barred federal courts from invalidating maps solely because they unfairly favor one political party, deprived "masses of citizens" of their "rights to voting equality."
Kagan suggested that the influx of gerrymandered maps is "driving people away from the center toward the wings, toward the extremes.
"Making what I think is, unfortunately, a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said.

Kagan also criticized rulings from the previous term, including the court’s decision limiting campaign finance restrictions and its ruling that made it more difficult to draw majority-minority congressional districts under the Voting Rights Act .
"Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said.

"I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should."
DESANTIS SIGNS FLORIDA REDISTRICTING MAP TO POTENTIALLY FLIP 4 HOUSE SEATS RED
Last term, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on how much state and national political parties could spend in coordination with their candidates.

Meanwhile, Kagan argued in dissent that the limits were necessary to prevent wealthy donors from working around direct contribution caps and that striking them down effectively allowed a political party to become an "alternative checking account" for a candidate.
"The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare," Kagan said. "And they’re right."
Kagan, who was appointed to the court by President Barack Obama in 2010, argued that it was in a much better position when there was greater ideological balance.

"There was a period of time where the court was in a better place, and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced, and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party," she said. "And the court had a kind of legitimacy. When the court has a legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country."

However, Kagan pushed back against the characterization that the conservative-leaning court simply rubber-stamped Trump's entire agenda. She pointed to previous rulings by the high court rejecting birthright citizenship restrictions, tariffs and Trump's restrictions on mail-in voting .
"It’s why the president sometimes really has not very nice things to say about the court’s decisions and some of my colleagues," Kagan said.

articles.headline: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
keyFacts: Students in Albania are clashing almost daily with police amid nearly five months of escalating anti-government protests.
Demonstrators demand the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, protesting government corruption, mismanaged universities, and rising education costs.
Prime Minister Rama claimed that foreign governments and antifa stoked the unrest, which he labeled a hybrid war.
body: The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.
Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."
She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."
Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."
Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.
"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."
This article was translated from German.

articles.headline: Cormac McCarthy’s The Road Is on Sale for $1.99 on Kindle
keyFacts: Cormac McCarthy's novel The Road is on sale for $1.99 on Amazon's Kindle platform.
The 2007 Pulitzer Prize-winning book follows a father and son surviving in a post-apocalyptic America.
McCarthy, known for other works like Blood Meridian and No Country for Old Men, died in 2023.
body: Wouldn’t it be nice to curl up with a good book right about now? If you use the Kindle ebook platform, you can pick up one of my all-time favorite novels on sale right now for just $1.99. It’s The Road, by Cormac McCarthy, and you can get it at Amazon for barely any money at all. It tells the story of a father and his son trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic America that’s been scorched of nearly all other life.

McCarthy is known for having dense, poetic prose, but he’s at his most readable in The Road. The book is comprised of many short sections, often just a paragraph long, with plenty of white space between each one. Here’s a scene-setting excerpt from near the beginning:

“With the first gray light he rose and left the boy sleeping and walked out to the road and squatted and studied the country to the south. Barren, silent, godless. He thought the month was October but he wasnt sure. He hadnt kept a calendar for years. They were moving south. There’d be no surviving another winter here.”

Notice the lack of apostrophes in some of the words. McCarthy famously doesn’t use quotation marks, either, but you almost always know who’s speaking. The sparse punctuation and the occasional unusual word choice create a unique tone in all of his work.

But whereas some of his other books, like Blood Meridian (often considered his masterpiece), are almost plotless and endlessly violent, The Road tells a simpler story of survival that's easy to follow. It has characters you can root for, even if a major victory is just them discovering unopened canned food in an abandoned cellar.

The Road won the 2007 Pulitzer Prize for fiction and went on to be turned into a movie starring Viggo Mortensen (the book is way better). It's one of his most popular novels; others include No Country for Old Men and All the Pretty Horses.
McCarthy was famously reclusive, rarely agreeing to be interviewed, but Oprah picked The Road for her book club and scored one of those rare interviews .

Cormac McCarthy died in 2023, but he carved out a singular voice in American fiction. I’ve read about half of his books, and of those, I’d say The Road is by far the best entry point into his work. I can't recommend it highly enough, especially for $1.99.

articles.headline: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
keyFacts: Meta agreed to a new stock deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to keep him from leaving California over a proposed state billionaire tax.
The agreement provides Zuckerberg with more Meta shares and quarterly selling rights to offset potential personal losses from a one-time 5% state tax.
Meta stated the eight-year deal is critically important to maintain Zuckerberg's leadership in California during ongoing industry transformations related to artificial intelligence.
body: - Published
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.

The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (Â£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.

Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.

Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.

Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
'Critically important'

Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.

After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.

It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.

And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

articles.headline: New York and T-Mobile Settle Dispute Over 4G Plan Price Hikes. How to Get a Credit
keyFacts: T-Mobile settled with the New York State Attorney General’s Office over claims the carrier violated price guarantees on 4G plans.
New York Attorney General Letitia James stated that T-Mobile raised rates in 2024 by about $5 per line after promising not to.
Affected customers have 45 days after notification to choose between canceling for a credit and gift card or staying for phone upgrades.
body: T-Mobile has come to an agreement with the New York State Attorney General’s Office over claims that the carrier did not honor price guarantees for T-Mobile One plans on its 4G network between January 2017 and April 2019. Those plans were advertised as being “Price Guarantee Plans.”
Affected active T-Mobile customers who leave the carrier will be able to collect a credit worth the last month’s payment and a $25 gift card.

Those who stay on and are still using an older phone can get a free 5G phone (worth up to $250) or credit up to $150 toward a more expensive 5G phone for lines that are still using 3G or 4G. Rates for their recurring monthly plans will stay the same until 2029.
More from CNET
As part of the agreement, T-Mobile is also making a one-time payment to the Attorney General’s office in the amount of around $98,000.

According to a press release issued by New York Attorney General Letitia James, an investigation by the office found that T-Mobile raised rates on those plans in 2024 by approximately $5 per line, a change that affected approximately 252,957 plans at the time. It also pegs the relief to be worth around $38 million in value.

“T-Mobile misled hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers by promising that it would never raise prices on their cellphone plans, only to do exactly that just a few years later,” said James in the release. “Consumers shouldn’t have to pay the price for a misleading sale.”

The office’s filed agreement notes that T-Mobile made the price guarantee in at least two press releases and during a CNET video interview with then-CEO John Legere in 2017. In that video, Legere said, “We also extended the Un-contract to T-Mobile One Unlimited, which means we will never raise your rate; we guarantee.”

The agreement notes that T-Mobile ran afoul of a New York State law that requires companies to disclose terms “clearly and conspicuously,” and that any disclaimers about the price guarantee were ineffective by “directly contradict[ing] what a reasonable consumer would understand the Price Guarantee Offer to mean.”
It also states that “Respondent [T-Mobile] neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Findings” that detail the investigation’s conclusions.

When asked about the agreement, T-Mobile sent the following statement to CNET: “The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments. The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”

Per the agreement, T-Mobile has 150 days starting Oct. 20 to identify and notify customers who are eligible for the relief. After they’ve been notified, customers will have 45 days to decide whether to cancel their T-Mobile account (getting the last month’s payment and a $25 cash card) or continue as a customer (getting a free or discounted 5G-capable phone for each affected line or the $150 credit toward a new phone). For the latter, T-Mobile will also not charge any costs such as transfer or activation fees.

articles.headline: Cordina agrees terms to fight Pacquiao, 47, on Fury-Joshua card
keyFacts: Promoter Eddie Hearn confirmed that former world champion Joe Cordina has agreed terms to fight 47-year-old boxing great Manny Pacquiao.
The potential bout is being negotiated for the undercard of the Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua heavyweight fight scheduled in Cardiff on December 11.
Hearn stated that while terms have been agreed from their side, it is not yet certain if the fight will ultimately happen.
body: - Published
Boxing great Manny Pacquiao, 47, could be added to the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua undercard - with former world champion Joe Cordina having agreed terms as his opponent.
Fury and Joshua are set to meet in an all-British heavyweight battle at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
Now promoter Eddie Hearn has confirmed that negotiations for a mouth-watering fight on the undercard are at an advanced stage.
"We've agreed terms to face Pacquiao, but we don't know if it's happening," Hearn revealed at a media event on Thursday.
"From our side, we've agreed to do it."

Tickets for Fury-Joshua sold out in just one hour, and fight fans could now also be able to see iconic eight-weight world champion Pacquiao face Wales' former super-featherweight world champion Cordina.
Pacquiao is regarded as one of the best boxers of all time, and it would be the first time the 12-time former champion has fought in the UK.
Details of other fights on the eagerly anticipated clash are yet to be released.
Pacquiao has not fought since July 2025, having returned from his second attempt at retirement.
But the Filipino icon would still be a draw for the huge television audience expected for the fight, that will be broadcast globally by streaming giants Netflix.
But the emergence of Cardiff-born Cordina, 34, as an opponent will also provide a hometown flavour to the show.
A former IBF super-featherweight champion, Cordina had been scheduled to face American Abduallah Mason for the WBO lightweight title in Cleveland in July when he was denied a US visa.
Cordina had remained in training while standing trial for allegations of assault, eventually being cleared of all charges.
That verdict has paved the way for a place on the Joshua-Fury bill, with Cordina eager to resume his career on what would be a huge opportunity in his own city.
It would be the first time Pacquiao has faced a British opponent since he beat Ricky Hatton in Las Vegas in 2009.
Pacquiao's last fight was a failed bid to take Mario Barrios' welterweight title, the bout ending in a majority draw four years after retiring to focus on politics in is homeland.
He has a record of 62 wins from 73 fights and had been scheduled to face unbeaten Floyd Mayweather in September, but the rematch of their 2015 meeting was postponed indefinitely in June.
Cordina has previously fought on the undercard of Fury's first fight with Oleksandr Usyk, losing his IBF title to Belfast's Anthony Cacace in Riyadh in May 2024.
It would represent the former Olympian's first fight in Cardiff since he regained the belt against Shavkat Rahimov the previous year.
